PlainTicker, the logo

There was no logo, so three launcher icons were designed without one and all three were rejected. This round designs the logo first: a wordmark, a mark, two lockups, and a launcher icon that is the same drawing rather than a different one. Two critics were run against it, Antigravity and Codex, and they are quoted in full at the bottom, unedited, including where they contradict each other and where they contradict me.

The logo

The mark, the wordmark, and the horizontal lockup. This is the thing.

The mark is three registered places on a row: two hold a figure and the third is kept, drawn and left empty. It is the app's one distinctive act, the refusal to print a figure it cannot stand behind, drawn as a place that stays in the row. Its figure blocks stand at the wordmark's cap height and its registers hang below the wordmark's baseline, the way a descender does, so the mark meets the word by a typographic rule rather than by a ratio picked by eye.

The wordmark

Three settings were drawn. Both critics killed the interesting one and they were right.

Plain in Outfit, Ticker in JetBrains Mono

Rejected by both critics.

The app's own law on its own name: words are Outfit, tickers are mono. The name is one word made of two kinds of object and it is set as two kinds of object. Cap heights are matched so the two halves share one cap line rather than reading as an accident.

Antigravity: “It is two fonts in a logo wearing a justification.” Codex found the defect in the argument rather than in the drawing: “‘Ticker’ is a word, not a ticker symbol.” The rule the setting claimed to apply is about ticker symbols and numerals, and the second half of the name is neither.

What the TopBar ships today at 15/600. One face, no argument, and nothing in it says what the product does.

One face, one name. It carries no idea, and after the split setting was killed that is the correct division of labour: the wordmark is the name and the mark is the idea.

bars vary in height to carry a quantity and these are two identical blocks over three identical registers, so they are places rather than values; the third register is drawn and empty, which is a reserved slot and not a missing bar. The third row of that table is the round's own finding. Attempts three, four and five only ever asked one ground question, Canvas or an Accent field, and every round took the Accent field and paid for it by knocking the mark out, which flattens a two-colour mark into a single silhouette. A cool off-white field reads 16.89 against Photos's 18.06, and it is the only treatment that keeps the mark's two-colour structure.

The two critics, in their own words

Neither block below has been edited, tightened, reordered or paraphrased. My adjudication is underneath and nothing above it is mine.

Google Antigravity

gemini-3.1-pro-high, effort high, plan mode, sandbox, 48.1 s, 23,401 tokens, one turn

1. It is two fonts in a logo wearing a justification. It relies on an intellectual argument the user cannot see to excuse a visual fracture they cannot ignore. In a headline, the sudden mid-word switch looks like a rendering glitch; in a row of running text, the mismatched rhythms arrest the eye; in a browser tab, the differing optical weights collapse into illegible noise. I would ship the whole name in Outfit for all three environments. The app's name is a word, so it must follow the typographic law for words.

2. short-measure ships, and it genuinely answers Codex's objection. kept-place merely shows that a figure is missing, which a user could misinterpret as an error, a loading state, or an alignment issue. short-measure draws the exact mathematical failure that caused the refusal. By placing the inadequate depth directly beneath the void, it explicitly proves that the foundation cannot justify the weight of a printed figure.

3. The edge is not worth abandoning the Canvas ground. The app's core identity relies on its stark, zero-radius, terminal-like objectivity. Wrapping that uncompromising interior in a #F2F5F8 light tile solely to satisfy a contrast metric is a false promise that reduces PlainTicker to the visual idiom of a generic calendar or calculator app. If the Canvas ground bleeds into a dark drawer and loses the superellipse mask, that borderless darkness is a truer expression of the product than a bright, safe paper wrapper.

4. The claim does not survive. As established in the fifth round, an inverted mark knocked out of a field loses its identity and reads only as a physical cut or a sidebar. If the geometry is no longer recognizable as a gauge, the marketing copy is defending a ghost. The replacement sentence is: *"The brand mark is the refusal itself: the deliberate empty space left behind when a pool is too thin to track."*

5.
First: short-measure.
Second: kept-place.
Third: withheld-print.
Fourth: floor.
Fifth: overhang.
Sixth: overhang-flush.

The one thing that will make a stranger misread your top choice (short-measure) in the first half second is its structural resemblance to a cellular signal-strength meter.

6. Change the height of the Accent stub to 4.

Codex

codex-cli 0.154.0, non-interactive, read-only, with the three rendered sheets attached as images

1. The split reads as two fonts in a logo. At headline size, the seam divides a dense, rounded “Plain” from a wider, mechanically spaced “Ticker.” Matching cap heights does not match their texture. The justification also misapplies the product’s typography rule: “Ticker” is a word, not a ticker symbol. In running text, the switch becomes an interruption within the name. In a browser tab, where the title uses browser typography, the distinction disappears entirely; the name must work without it. I would ship the all-Outfit setting. It reads as one name, and the product can establish its numerical typography where actual numbers appear.

2. Short-measure does not answer the earlier objection. It shows a third bar with a smaller value. Nothing in the drawing establishes that the stub measures support while the tall bars represent readings supported by something else. They occupy the same baseline and use the same rectangular vocabulary, so the eye assigns them the same kind of quantity. Your explanation supplies the causal relationship; the mark supplies a bar chart. Worse, the product refuses to print an unreliable figure, while this mark visibly prints a small figure. The empty area above it is ordinary chart background, not an observable act of withholding. The exaggerated scale is secondary to that categorical mistake.

3. Kept-place survives reduction better. At the smaller size, its blue segment remains a clean ending to the baseline; short-measure adds a tiny step that reads as a low bar or a rendering irregularity. But kept-place does not visibly reserve a third place. There is no repeated container, divider or other structure making that empty region a slot. There are two uprights and an extended foot. The cleaner mark therefore loses the claimed explanation, but short-measure never secured that explanation either. This is a choice between a cleaner generic symbol and a more explicit chart—not between two successful drawings of refusal.

4. The paper field provides a boundary and disguises the tile within the drawer’s prevailing treatment. Those are different outcomes, and the contrast measurement establishes only the first. The paper version is plainly easier to locate than the Canvas version. But beside the other light tiles, its identity must come from the interior mark, and that is where this candidate remains weak. Preserving two colours preserves a small blue terminal; it does not make that terminal meaningful. Also, the paper treatment preserves the two-colour structure, not literally Ink and Accent: the main strokes become dark. Ship paper for visibility, but stop treating its contrast ratio as evidence of distinctiveness.

5. Overhang reads as an off-centre capital T or a top-alignment control. Overhang-flush reads as a thick upper-left corner or crop bracket. Floor reads as a top rule with a detached insertion cursor beneath it. Kept-place reads as a pause button resting on a tray; the blue ending looks like a status attachment. Short-measure reads as a bar-chart or equalizer control. Withheld-print reads as a selected text cursor in the large field and an outlined zero in the narrow lockup. Its changing outer proportions make that association unstable. Of these six, overhang is furthest from a familiar system control as drawn: its imbalance gives it a particular silhouette. That distance still does not communicate inadequate backing.

6. The tracking-gauge sentence fails. At the larger size, gauge-inverted looks like a chart-axis fragment with an intersecting cross. At the smaller size, it becomes a compact arrangement of ticks without a readable measurement. There is no reference, range or relationship that identifies tracking, much less tracking a token against its underlying stock. The blue field improves visibility without improving that explanation. “Nobody else has” is an unsupported exclusivity claim, and “says what the app does” assigns the drawing information it does not contain. Replace the sentence with: “The brand mark is an abstract symbol derived from the app’s tracking gauge.”

7. Set the kept-place mark’s height in the horizontal lockup to exactly 1.00 times the wordmark’s cap height, scaling it uniformly and retaining its current vertical centring. That is the drawing I would ship with the all-Outfit wordmark and paper launcher field. The current oversized symbol gives a generic pause-and-tray shape more authority than its meaning earns.

Adjudication

Mine. Everything above it is theirs.

Where they agree, which is the settled part of the round. Both critics killed the split
wordmark, both declared the tracking-gauge sentence dead, and neither disputed a single
measurement. The split wordmark is the one I brought into the round believing in, and Codex did not
kill it on taste, it found the defect in the argument: the design system's rule is that *ticker
symbols* and numerals are set in the monospace face, and "Ticker" in the product's name is an
English word, not a ticker symbol. The setting claimed to apply a rule it did not apply. That is
not a matter of preference and there is nothing to weigh against it. The whole name is set in
Outfit.

Where they disagree, first: which mark. Antigravity ranks short-measure first and says it
"genuinely answers Codex's objection ... it explicitly proves that the foundation cannot justify
the weight of a printed figure." Codex, which wrote that objection, says it does not: "the product
refuses to print an unreliable figure, while this mark visibly prints a small figure. The empty
area above it is ordinary chart background, not an observable act of withholding."

I follow Codex, and not because it owns the sentence. Its reason is checkable against the product
rather than against a taste. Below $10,000 of pool the app prints nothing at all; it does not print
a small number. A mark that draws a short bar in the third place depicts a behaviour this app does
not have, and it depicts it in the one place the app is unlike every neighbour it will sit beside.
Antigravity's reading requires the viewer to know that the stub measures support while the two tall
blocks measure readings, and nothing in the drawing says so: same baseline, same vocabulary, same
kind of quantity. Short-measure is out.

Where they disagree, second: the ground. Antigravity says keep the Canvas near-black: "if the
Canvas ground bleeds into a dark drawer and loses the superellipse mask, that borderless darkness
is a truer expression of the product than a bright, safe paper wrapper." Codex says ship paper for
visibility and stop treating a contrast ratio as evidence of distinctiveness.

I follow Codex. Antigravity's answer is an aesthetic preference set against a measurement, and the
measurement is the one thing three rounds of this have produced: 1.03 to 1 is not a dark tile, it
is no tile, and attempt three's compositor could not locate PlainTicker's own slot in the
screenshot by scanning because there was nothing there to find. A brand argument whose conclusion
is that the icon should be invisible in the drawer is not a brand argument. Codex's caveat is
adopted rather than argued with, and it corrects my own wording: on paper the mark does not keep
Ink and Accent literally, the strokes become dark ink, so what survives is the two-colour
structure, and 16.89 to 1 buys a boundary and not distinctiveness. Distinctiveness has to come from
the drawing.

The change that mattered was not either critic's asked-for change. It was one sentence of
Codex's reasoning: kept-place "does not visibly reserve a third place. There is no repeated
container, divider or other structure making that empty region a slot." That is correct about the
drawing it saw, where the row was one continuous rule with a blue end, and it is the difference
between a mark that means something and a mark with a caption. The row is now three separate
registers on the same pitch as the places above them: two carry a figure and the third is drawn,
registered and empty. A battery has one container. No chart draws the register of a value it does
not have.

Both asked-for changes are drawn and neither is adopted as stated.

Antigravity asked for the Accent stub at 4 units instead of 8. It is drawn as short-measure-agy,
rendered at every size and measured in the drawer. Four units is 3.4dp and 10 device pixels on the
Seeker tile, under the 6-unit floor this repository has enforced since attempt one, whose 2-unit
tick was 1.3dp and was simply not present on the phone. Halving the only element that carries the
meaning is attempt one with a different number on it, and it is applied to a drawing that lost on
other grounds anyway.

Codex asked for the mark at exactly 1.00 of the wordmark's cap height in the horizontal lockup. It
is drawn, and it was aimed at a mark that no longer exists: the "pause-and-tray" shape it was
correcting is the continuous row that Codex's own paragraph five got rid of. What the instruction
encodes, that the mark had more authority than its meaning earns, is taken, but by a rule rather
than by a number: the mark's figure blocks now stand at exactly the wordmark's cap height and its
registers hang below the wordmark's baseline the way a descender does, which puts the mark 1.294
cap heights tall overall. Codex can still say that is 29 percent too much. Both drawings are on
this page and the founder can see the argument rather than read it.

The claim in .agents/product-marketing.md does not survive. "The brand mark is the tracking
gauge itself rather than a letter, because it is the one mark nobody else has and it says what the
app does." Both critics rejected it independently, having seen the gauge inverted and given the
edge it never had. Codex: "There is no reference, range or relationship that identifies tracking
... 'nobody else has' is an unsupported exclusivity claim, and 'says what the app does' assigns the
drawing information it does not contain." Antigravity: "the marketing copy is defending a ghost."

The deeper reason, which neither critic needed and which decides it anyway: the gauge is drawn only
above the liquidity floor. Below $10,000 of pool the app does not draw it. A brand mark cannot be
the one element the product withholds; it has to be the thing that is true of every screen. What is
always true is the withholding itself. Both critics offered a replacement sentence and Antigravity's
is the better one, so it is the one proposed:

> The brand mark is the refusal itself: the deliberate empty space left behind when a pool is too
> thin to track.
